concept.text: A proof or disproof that every nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function has real part 1/2. Sources given: https://www.claymath.org/millennium-problems/ ; https://world-of-mathematics.com/blog/millennium-problems-overview/.

change_log.change: Added by hand to MAT on 2026-11-14.
change_log.reason: Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problem; added at the owner's request, November 14, 2026.

page.title: Resolution of the Riemann hypothesis
page.definition: A proof or disproof settles whether every zero s of the Riemann zeta function ζ(s) in 0 < Re(s) < 1 has Re(s) = 1/2. Here ζ is the meromorphic continuation of ∑n≥1 n⁻ˢ from Re(s) > 1; zeros in that strip are called nontrivial.

goal.need: Resolving the hypothesis decides whether π(x) = Li(x) + O(√x log x) as x → ∞, where π(x) counts primes at most x and Li(x) is the logarithmic integral. This bounds the error in approximating prime counts by a constant times √x log x for sufficiently large x. Clay selected the hypothesis as one of seven Millennium Prize Problems announced on 24 May 2000.

statements.quote: to emphasize the importance of working towards a solution of the deepest, most difficult problems
statements.context: One stated purpose of the Millennium Prize Problems, which include the Riemann hypothesis.

statements.body: Clay Mathematics Institute, official problem description by Enrico Bombieri
statements.quote: The failure of the Riemann hypothesis would create havoc in the distribution of prime numbers.

completion.title: Clay accepts a complete resolution of the Riemann hypothesis after its Millennium Prize examination.
completion.criterion: CMI determines that a complete mathematical solution satisfactorily answers its official Riemann hypothesis problem. The solution must appear in a Qualifying Outlet, survive at least two years of community examination, gain general acceptance, and pass CMI examination. A proof must cover every nontrivial zero; a counterexample must effectively resolve the problem under §5(c)(i). CMI’s examination includes a committee of at least three members, including at least two experts in the problem’s area.
completion.set_by: Clay Mathematics Institute, Millennium Prize Description and Rules, §§4–7, adopted on 26 September 2018.
completion.threshold_quote: Second, a Proposed Solution must satisfy examination by CMI.
completion.basis: Clay supplies an external acceptance procedure for the complete mathematical problem and explicitly addresses counterexamples. Its rules distinguish community acceptance from its subsequent examination. Its Riemann hypothesis page continues to classify the problem as unsolved.

milestones.title: A proof establishes infinitely many zeta zeros with real part 1/2.
milestones.criterion: Prove that for every T > 0 there exists a real t > T with ζ(1/2 + it) = 0. Hardy announced this result on 6 April 1914. Hardy and Littlewood’s 1916 paper, §1.4, recalls the theorem using the completed function Ξ(t), whose real zeros correspond to zeta zeros on Re(s) = 1/2.
milestones.set_by: Analytic number theory’s convention of proved partial results; Hardy’s theorem, recalled and developed by Hardy and Littlewood in Acta Mathematica (1916), §1.4.
milestones.threshold_quote: has an infinity of real zeros.

milestones.title: A proof places more than five-twelfths of nontrivial zeta zeros on the critical line.
milestones.criterion: Prove κ = lim inf as T → ∞ of N₀(T)/N(T) > 5/12, where N counts nontrivial zeros with 0 < Im(s) ≤ T and N₀ counts those on Re(s) = 1/2, with multiplicity. Pratt, Robles, Zaharescu and Zeindler proved κ > 0.417293; their article appeared online on 6 December 2019. A preprint revised on 19 August 2026 claims a proportion of at least 0.6725 for simple zeros on the line; that claim is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: The field’s asymptotic zero-proportion benchmark, instantiated by Pratt, Robles, Zaharescu and Zeindler, Theorem 1.2.
milestones.threshold_quote: More than five-twelfths of the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta-function are on the critical line.

milestones.title: Rigorous computation verifies every zeta zero up to height 3,000,175,332,800 on the critical line.
milestones.criterion: Establish that every nontrivial zero β + iγ with 0 < γ ≤ 3,000,175,332,800 has β = 1/2, including certification that no zeros were missed. Platt and Trudgian verified this with interval arithmetic: the lowest 12,363,153,437,138 positive-ordinate zeros satisfy the test. Height is the dimensionless imaginary part γ. The journal article was first published on 22 January 2021.
milestones.set_by: The field’s finite-height verification convention, instantiated by Platt and Trudgian, Theorem 1.
milestones.threshold_quote: The Riemann hypothesis is true up to height 3 000 175 332 800.

milestones.title: A complete resolution survives two years of examination and gains general mathematical acceptance.
milestones.criterion: A complete proposed resolution gains general acceptance in the global mathematics community, as determined by CMI, after surviving rigorous community examination for at least two years. At least two years must also have elapsed since publication in a Qualifying Outlet. This is the first evaluation stage under §7(a)(i), preceding examination by CMI itself.
milestones.set_by: Clay Mathematics Institute, Millennium Prize Description and Rules, §§4(a–c) and 7(a)(i).
milestones.threshold_quote: general acceptance in the global mathematics community

not_found: No prescribed sequence of intermediate zero-height or zero-proportion targets was found in Clay’s official problem description or prize rules.
Wiley redirected requests for the Platt–Trudgian full text to its abstract; the numerical theorem was available in the authors’ arXiv manuscript.

results.finding: Hardy and Littlewood prove that infinitely many zeta zeros lie on the line Re(s) = 1/2.
results.detail: The authors report their own proof of a zero in an interval beginning at T for every sufficiently large T. The interval’s upper bound is garbled in the supplied text.

results.finding: Nontrivial Riemann zeta zeros; asymptotic population, no finite sample: κ > 0.417293.
results.detail: The bound is unconditional and exceeds five-twelfths.
results.quote: More than five-twelfths of the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta-function are on the critical line.

results.finding: Nontrivial zeta zeros, asymptotic count: at least 0.67353820 are simple and on the critical line.
results.detail: The claimed lower bound exceeds 5/12. This is an unreviewed preprint; its formal proof relies on computed statements whose runs Lean's kernel does not check.
results.quote: More than 83.9% of the zeros of the Riemann zeta function are distinct and more than 67.35% are simple and on the critical line

results.finding: Riemann zeta nontrivial zeros, asymptotically: κ ≥ 0.673639287955244058993397664145.
results.detail: The source reports a machine-checked proof; independent expert review is not recorded.

results.finding: The lowest 12,363,153,437,138 nontrivial zeta zeros lie on the critical line, through height 3,000,175,332,800.
results.detail: The authors report rigorous numerical verification and use a variation of Turing’s method to account for all expected zeros. This source is the authors’ preprint.
results.quote:
Theorem 1. The Riemann hypothesis is true up to height 3 000 175 332 800. That is, the
lowest 12 363 153 437 138 non-trivial zeroes ρ have ℜρ = 1/2.
